case_info.explanation: C. Perform an excisional biopsy Excisional biopsy (C) is the optimal choice for this patient, as it allows for definitive histopathological examination of the nodule, particularly considering the patient’s history of ulcerative colitis and the presence of telangiectasia. Initiating topical mitomycin C (A) may be less appropriate, as it typically is used for confirmed ocular surface neoplasia, and using it without a definitive diagnosis could lead to inappropriate treatment and delay proper management. Starting systemic corticosteroids (B) usually is not ideal without clear evidence of systemic inflammation or an acute flare of ulcerative colitis and could mask the underlying condition. Finally, observing and following up in 3 months, while not an unreasonable option given the patient’s lack of symptoms, risks delaying the diagnosis of a potentially serious condition, such as a malignant neoplasm. Given the ease of an excisional biopsy and its ability to provide an immediate and accurate diagnosis, option C is likely the most appropriate approach. The biopsy revealed a monoclonal CD5+ small B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder, favoring small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry showed CD20+ cells with co-expression of CD5, CD43, and BCL2, and negative results for CD3, CD10, BCL1, and SOX11. CD23 expression was noted in rare cells. Ophthalmic adnexal lymphoma (OAL) is the most common malignant neoplasm involving the ocular adnexa and representing 11% to 24% of all ocular tumors. Primary OALs are rare, accounting for 8% of extranodal lymphomas, and as many as 20% primary conjunctival lymphomas may develop into systemic disease over time, although this may be months or even years later.1-3The most common subtypes include extranodal marginal zone lymphomas of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) (35%-80%), followed by follicular lymphoma (approximately 20%) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (approximately 8%).4Ocular adnexal SLL are rarer, with few reported cases.5,6 While less is known about ocular SLL specifically, predisposing factors for OAL, specifically MALT and DLBCL, include autoimmune conditions (eg, Sjögren syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease, systemic lupus erythematosus), immune deficiency or dysfunction, infectious etiologies (Chlamydiaspp andHelicobacter pylori), and prior radiation exposure.7-9This patient had a history of ulcerative colitis, which may bolster the link between autoimmune disease and conjunctival lymphoma. Treatment of OAL primarily depends on the extent of periocular or systemic involvement. For localized disease, complete surgical resection or external localized beam radiation therapy is often used. However, ocular SLL has an increased risk of extranodal metastases on presentation.5,6In these cases, therapy is not standardized; however, rituximab is commonly used, particularly if the tumor is large, infiltrative, and nonresectable. In our case, a complete excisional biopsy was performed with no evidence of recurrence. Nonetheless, long-term follow up is crucial, as patients with OAL and prior CLL or SLL demonstrated an increased incidence in both hematologic and solid secondary primary malignant neoplasms.10 Following a complete excisional biopsy, follow-up visits revealed no recurrence of ocular disease and good visual acuity (20/32) in the left eye. The patient was referred to hematology, and subsequent positron emission tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging orbits on last follow-up 8 months after excisional biopsy revealed no signs of systemic malignant neoplasm.

Ophthalmic adnexal lymphoma (OAL) is the most common malignant neoplasm involving the ocular adnexa and representing 11% to 24% of all ocular tumors. Primary OALs are rare, accounting for 8% of extranodal lymphomas, and as many as 20% primary conjunctival lymphomas may develop into systemic disease over time, although this may be months or even years later.1-3The most common subtypes include extranodal marginal zone lymphomas of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) (35%-80%), followed by follicular lymphoma (approximately 20%) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (approximately 8%).4Ocular adnexal SLL are rarer, with few reported cases.5,6 While less is known about ocular SLL specifically, predisposing factors for OAL, specifically MALT and DLBCL, include autoimmune conditions (eg, Sjögren syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease, systemic lupus erythematosus), immune deficiency or dysfunction, infectious etiologies (Chlamydiaspp andHelicobacter pylori), and prior radiation exposure.7-9This patient had a history of ulcerative colitis, which may bolster the link between autoimmune disease and conjunctival lymphoma.
